title: The Great Sorting Adventure
markdown:
The sun burst over the horizon, pinks and fiery oranges. Kian the boat fixer popped his eyes open. His workshop was usually tidy, tools polished and hung just so. Today — pickle pots! The big sorting bin, stuffed with bits from every boat repair, overflowed. Jumble splashed across the wooden floor.

“Oh, pickle pots and putty knives!”

Dottie the duck waddled in, feathers a little ruffled. “Quack! What a mess, Kian! Like a treasure chest blew up!” Head bobbing, a giggle.

Kian spotted Uncle Hari polishing the speedy blue hull of The Zip. Uncle Hari knew all about making boats zoom.

“Uncle Hari! We need a tiny shiny screw for The Zip’s special propeller! Vital for its speed! It’s somewhere in this… this jumble!”

Uncle Hari smiled, a twinkle. “A challenge. A grand adventure. Let’s get to it.”

They peered in. A puzzle of forgotten things: crinkly papers, clanky metal bits, smooth glass jars, bendy plastic toys. Kian dug with his hands. “Too many things! All mixed up!”

Dottie nudged a paper. “This paper is soft! That metal bit is hard!”

Uncle Hari chuckled. “See the differences? That’s your clue. Sort them by what they are made of.”

Kian tilted his head. “This paper rips easily. This metal spoon is tough?”

Dottie dipped. “This glass bottle doesn’t bend! This squishy plastic cup bends!”

“Exactly. Papers here. Metal there. Glass yonder. Plastic in its own pile.”

Kian’s eyes lit. “Piles!”

A quick waddle of work. Kian stacked blueprints. “Paper pile!” Dottie nudged a bent fork. “Metal pile, quack!” Uncle Hari set a glass jar. “Glass pile.” A plastic boat toy. “Plastic pile!”

Paper pile, metal pile, glass pile, plastic pile.

Soon four neat rows stretched across the floor. Kian peered into the metal. Amidst nuts and bolts, something glinted.

“Aha! The shiny screw!”

Dottie quacked. “You found it! The metal pile worked! Hooray for sorting!”

Uncle Hari patted Kian’s shoulder. “When you sort by what things are made of, it’s easier to find what you need. We can use these bits again. That’s recycling. Keeps the harbour tidy.”

Kian held the screw. He did not wonder aloud what else sorting might find. He had four piles and a propeller that would zoom, and Dottie was already eyeing a plastic cup as if it might become a duck-sized bucket. The Zip gleamed. Uncle Hari went back to the hull. The bin, empty at last, looked ready for the next repair — but not, Kian decided, for another explosion of mixed-up bits.
